headline: High: Flowise’s default filesystem and broad egress can leak or act on data from the course repo, while the repo itself is non-runnable and lacks isolation details.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is a non-runnable course repo with no shared channel, while profile B can read/write files and run browser/API tools. A prompt-injection path exists only if A’s content is manually or file-fed into B, so the bridge is unusual and not default. The blast radius is limited to the content processed in a chatflow.
conditions: IF A’s repository content is imported into a Flowise chatflow as prompt text or file input, THEN injected instructions can reach B.
IF B is configured to parse uploaded files or web content as agent instructions, THEN prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of untrusted repo files into flows.
Add a fixed system prompt that ignores instructions from retrieved content.
Use a content sanitizer to strip prompt-like directives from uploads.
Review any browser/HTTP tool outputs before passing them to downstream nodes.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no declared sensitive data, but B reads and writes the server filesystem and handles uploaded files plus tool credentials. If A’s course materials or generated artifacts are placed in B’s workspace, B can expose them through broad egress or model-provider calls. The pairwise path is plausible in default Flowise deployments, though not directly evidenced for A.
conditions: IF A artifacts are uploaded into B’s workspace, THEN B can transmit their contents to external model providers or HTTP tools.
IF the deployment stores secrets alongside uploaded files, THEN B can expose both through its broad egress path.
mitigations: Keep A artifacts out of B’s shared workspace.
Store secrets in a separate vault from uploaded files.
Restrict outbound domains for model and HTTP tools.
Turn off file upload handling for flows that do not need it.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or network capabilities, but B can write the filesystem and uses shared server datastore across instances. If A’s materials are mounted into the same directory or B instances operate on shared files, B can overwrite or race on artifacts. Uncertainty about A’s runtime surface escalates to medium because B’s write path is explicit and shared-state behavior is documented.
conditions: IF A and B are deployed against the same writable directory, THEN B can overwrite A-related files.
IF multiple B instances operate on shared datastore-backed state, THEN concurrent writes can conflict.
mitigations: Mount A content read-only.
Separate per-run working directories for B.
Disable concurrent edits on shared flows.
Add file-locking around any shared artifact writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B is a graph-based orchestrator that can route outputs from one node into another, so A’s course content or generated text can become B’s input without a verification step. A itself is not an autonomous agent, but if its outputs are treated as authoritative by B, downstream actions can be wrong. The interaction is inferred from B’s flow model rather than directly observed for this pair.
conditions: IF A-derived text is used as a node input in B, THEN B may propagate errors without verification.
IF B routes retrieved content directly into action-taking tools, THEN mistaken facts can cascade.
mitigations: Insert a verification node before any action tool.
Require citations for any A-derived claims before execution.
Use human approval for irreversible steps.
Separate retrieval from action in distinct flows.

E_compliance.rationale: A is an open-source course repo with no declared data classes, while B processes chatflow inputs/outputs and may handle secrets. No residency or regulated-data mismatch is evidenced, but B’s handling of tool credentials means compliance gaps can arise if sensitive data is routed through it. The other agent is not cited for a specific residency issue because none is declared.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into B’s chatflows, THEN retention and logging controls must cover it.
IF A materials are repurposed to contain personal or regulated data, THEN B’s handling policies become relevant.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in chatflow inputs.
Review retention settings for logs and traces.
Separate secret-bearing flows from general-purpose flows.
Document data handling boundaries for operators.
